title: Phrasal Verbs
subtitle: Two words that mean something neither one does.
objectives: Explain how the particle changes the meaning
Tell a phrasal verb from a verb plus preposition

cards.title: A small word can change a verb completely
cards.text: Take 'take'. Now take off, take up, take in, take over. Same verb, four unrelated meanings.

cards.title: A verb plus a particle, acting as one word
cards.text: The particle is a little word like up, off, out or into. Together they mean something new.
points: **give up** does not mean giving anything.
**look after** is not about looking.
**The meaning is in the pair**, not in the verb alone.
**That is why** you cannot translate them word by word.

cards.title: One verb, five particles
cards.text: Same verb every time. Tap through and watch the meaning change completely.

cards.title: Taking something apart has its own verbs
cards.text: Almost every step of a teardown is a phrasal verb, and swapping the particle changes the job.
points: **take apart** — dismantle it into pieces.
**take off** — remove one part, like the guard.
**put back** — return it to where it was.
**put together** — reassemble the whole thing.

question.explain: The particle 'apart' is doing all the work. 'Take off' would only remove one piece.

cards.title: Can you split it?
cards.text: A real phrasal verb often lets the object sit in the middle. A plain preposition never does.
points: **Turn the fan off** and **turn off the fan** are both fine.
**He ran up the hill** cannot become *he ran the hill up*.
**So 'ran up' there** is just a verb plus a preposition.
**If it splits**, it is usually a phrasal verb.

cards.title: The ones every pilot uses
cards.text: Flight vocabulary is unusually full of them, and the particles matter.
points: **take off** — leave the ground.
**touch down** — land.
**turn back** — abandon the route and return.
**hold off** — delay. Not the same as hold on.

question.text: You can work out a phrasal verb's meaning from the two words separately.
question.explain: Usually not. 'Give up' has nothing to do with giving. The pair carries its own meaning.

cards.title: Literature Review: Don Quixote, Chapter 13: In the Black Mountains
cards.text: Quixote decides to go into the mountains and do penance, mostly to prove he can.
points: **He took off** most of his clothes.
**He sent Sancho away** with a letter.
**He carried on** alone, performing madness deliberately.
**The chapter is thick** with phrasal verbs.

question.explain: A pronoun object must go in the middle: switched it off.

cards.title: Took it apart
cards.alt: A mechanical alarm clock taken apart with every component laid out in rows beside a small screwdriver
cards.text: Not "took it off" and not "took it up". The particle is doing all the work.

terms.def: A verb and a particle that together mean something new.
The small word — up, off, out, back — attached to the verb.
A phrasal verb that lets the object sit in the middle.
A word showing position or direction, not part of the verb.

cards.title: What to remember
points: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle, meaning something new.
The particle decides the meaning: take off, take apart, take over.
If the object can sit in the middle, it is usually phrasal.
A pronoun object always goes in the middle.

options: a verb plus a particle acting as one unit
quiz.explain: The pair carries a meaning neither word has alone.
A pronoun object sits in the middle.

quiz.text: 'Give up' is about giving something to someone.
quiz.explain: The pair means to quit. Neither word tells you that on its own.
quiz.objective: Explain how the particle changes the meaning

quiz.text: 'He ran up the hill' — is 'ran up' a phrasal verb here?
options: No, it is a verb plus a preposition
Yes, because it has two words
quiz.explain: You cannot say 'he ran the hill up', so it does not split. It is a preposition.
quiz.objective: Tell a phrasal verb from a verb plus preposition
Explain how the particle changes the meaning

quiz.explain: To delay or postpone. Different from hold on.

quiz.text: Changing the particle can completely change a phrasal verb's meaning.
quiz.explain: Take off, take apart, take over and take in share a verb and share nothing else.
quiz.objective: Explain how the particle changes the meaning

quiz.explain: Switch off splits around its object. The others cannot.
quiz.objective: Tell a phrasal verb from a verb plus preposition

quiz.text: In Chapter 13, Quixote goes into the mountains to…
quiz.explain: He performs a deliberate madness to prove his devotion, and sends Sancho off with a letter.

quiz.text: What does 'turn back' mean for a flight?
quiz.explain: Return to where it came from, abandoning the planned route.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 3 English. Phrasal verbs are introduced through the particle rather than the verb, because the particle is what carries the meaning — take off, take apart, take over — and that framing makes them learnable instead of arbitrary. The separability test is given as a practical way to tell a phrasal verb from a verb plus preposition, which is the distinction an exam will probe. Vocabulary is drawn from a teardown and from aviation, both of which use these constantly and both of which he already has words for.
discussion: Why can't you translate a phrasal verb word by word?
How does the splitting test work?
Which particle would you add to 'put' to mean reassemble?
extension: List every phrasal verb you use while taking something apart.
Find five in one page of Chapter 13.
misconceptions: Saying 'switched off it' instead of 'switched it off'.
Assuming any verb with a small word after it is phrasal.
